Subject: Scoped Ephemeral Handling & Audit Plan for MediCore — next steps

Hi Asha / Ravi — thanks again for the demo earlier. Quick recap from our side and proposed next steps so everyone is aligned.

Summary of requirements we heard on the call:
- PII scope: names, emails, patient IDs (hashed), device telemetry that may be indirectly identifying.
- Retention: primary ask — no persistence of user-provided prompt text in production logs (team referenced a 0-retention requirement for sensitive prompts).
- Observability: MediCore needs request-level success/failure metrics and token counts for billing, but wants them aggregated and redacted for PII.
- Residency: initial deployment in us-east, potential eu expansion later.

Options we can deliver (high level):
1) Ephemeral/0-retention mode for prompt & response text (recommended): keep KV/cache in-memory only, never write raw prompt/response to disk, no long-term token logs.
2) Short retention logs: store redacted request metadata (no raw text) for 7 days for debugging; full raw logs for 30 days only under explicit, audited incident workflows.
3) Custom differential retention: define data classes (S1: PII — 0 days; S2: hashed ids — 7 days; S3: telemetry/metrics — 90 days).

Action items I propose:
- We’ll deliver a technical design doc showing how ephemeral mode works and which observability hooks remain available (attached: ephemeral-mode-config.md).
- Aditya (security) will follow up with the minimal evidence set we can provide (SOC2 summary redacted, sample audit logs).
- Schedule a 30-minute security deep-dive next week to sign off on the dev/test plan and incident access process.

Next steps: can you confirm whether MediCore requires absolute zero write-to-disk under all circumstances (including transient cache persistence during autoscaling), or whether a short retention window for in-memory crash dumps is acceptable? If you prefer, we can map to the differential template above.

I’ll tentatively hold 30 minutes on Mon 26th or Tue 27th (PST) — what works best?

Thanks,

Thanks Vanessa — good summary. Short answers before we sync:
- Our compliance team is pushing for no raw prompt retention in production. They would consider a short, strictly in-memory crash dump retention only if it is encrypted in RAM and automatically zeroed on process restart.
- We still need aggregated metrics for cost allocation (per-team token counts) but those must not contain any raw prompts or full-response excerpts.
- Proof required: a security artifact showing the in-memory-only guarantee, plus a redacted SOC2 excerpt is helpful.

We'll plan for the Monday slot if possible. Ravi and I are flexible. Also attaching a short data-scope spreadsheet that lists the fields we consider sensitive (see MediCore-data-scope.xlsx).

Hi Asha — quick technical clarifications from security/research:
- Ephemeral mode: we can run an in-memory-only path that avoids writing prompt/response text to persistent storage. That applies to KV cache and request logs. However, when autoscaling causes processes to be preempted/serialised, we need to ensure the restart path does not persist the cached state; we accomplish this by never serializing sensitive fields and by flushing process memory on termination.
- Crash dumps: we can disable full crash dumps in production builds and enable a minimal, encrypted in-RAM transient dump for <72 hours that is only accessible through an audited incident access workflow. If MediCore requires 0 retention under all conditions, we can implement that, but it will limit our ability to debug rare production issues.

Deliverables we can provide before the security call:
- Redacted SOC2 excerpt (attached: SOC2-summary-redacted.pdf).
- Design note: ephemeral-mode-config.md (attached) showing how headers/metadata are retained for metrics while removing payloads.
- Sample aggregation output that shows token counts per tenant with no prompt snippet. (I will upload after this thread.)

Request for Asha: please confirm whether your compliance team will accept the encrypted-in-RAM crash dump for incident response, or if you require absolute prohibition of any transient dumps. If the latter, we’ll include that as a binding configuration in the dedicated deployment contract.

Thanks,
